title: RFID Card Factory Direct from China — Proud Tek Manufacturer Pricing
summary: Proud Tek is a direct RFID factory in Shenzhen — building cards, tags, labels and wristbands in-house since 2008 and shipping to buyers in 50+ countries — so a factory-direct order goes to the people who laminate, print and encode your product, at the factory-gate price with no trading-company markup in between. Chip sourcing, antenna bonding, printing, encoding, laser engraving, quality testing and export packing all run under one ISO 9001 management system, which is the difference between a factory and a reseller forwarding your purchase order. This page sets out the capability menu across product families, how buying direct compares with going through a trading company, and the certifications and QC records your procurement team can verify before the first order.
heroPoints: A direct factory, not a trading desk: cards, NFC tags, UHF labels and wristbands built across two Shenzhen sites and ten automated lines under one ISO 9001 system, so your order reaches the line that makes it.
Factory-gate pricing with no middleman — you pay the price a trading company would pay us, without the resale margin it adds for handling paperwork rather than manufacturing the product.

In-house from chip to carton: sourcing, antenna bonding, lamination, full-colour printing, encoding, laser engraving, 100% read-verification and export packing all happen under one roof, with the QC records to prove it.

brief.text: A Shenzhen RFID factory, direct since 2008, that makes and encodes cards, tags, labels and wristbands in-house and sells them at the factory-gate price — one supplier, one ISO 9001 management system, one point of accountability.

sections.title: What ordering factory-direct actually changes
sections.intro: 'Factory-direct' is the most-claimed and least-audited phrase in China RFID sourcing — plenty of storefronts using it are trading desks with a stock-photo factory. Proud Tek means it literally: we own the machines between your specification and your loading dock, which is why the [factory tour](/about/factory/) and audit are open invitations rather than awkward requests. Buying direct changes three things — who you talk to, what you pay, and who is accountable when a reader rejects a batch. The numbers below are the ones a procurement team checks first, and each is [independently verifiable](/about/certifications/).
bullets: You talk to the makers, not a middleman — application engineering, the quality team and the production planner are in the building, so a spec question or a delivery-date commitment does not travel through a sales intermediary first.
You pay the factory-gate price — the same price a trading company pays us before it adds a resale margin, so the layer that priced in someone else's overhead simply is not there.

Cost is itemised, not bundled — we break a quote into chip, antenna or inlay, card body or substrate, printing, encoding and packaging, so you can see where the money goes and trade specifications up or down with eyes open.

One roof, one system — chip sourcing, antenna bonding, lamination, printing, encoding, laser engraving, testing and export packing run under a single ISO 9001 management system rather than being subcontracted across a broker's suppliers.

Accountability has a name — a factory owns its defects; when a batch fails your reader, the engineers who built it retune and re-run it, instead of a reseller relaying the problem back to a plant it does not control.

bullets: RFID cards and fobs run to ISO/IEC 14443 (13.56 MHz) and ISO/IEC 11784/11785 (125 kHz LF); PVC, PET, ABS, polycarbonate, wood, metal and recycled bodies are all in-house, with offset or digital print and inkjet personalisation.

NFC stickers and tags use NTAG 213, NTAG 215 and NTAG 216 for URL, vCard and marketing taps, and NTAG 424 DNA when a label has to prove it is genuine with AES-128 SUN authentication (ISO/IEC 14443, NFC Forum); ICODE SLIX2 covers HF vicinity work to ISO/IEC 15693.
UHF inlays and labels use Impinj and NXP UCODE silicon to ISO/IEC 18000-63 / EPC Gen2v2 (860-960 MHz), encoded to the GS1 EPC Tag Data Standard for retail and logistics.

The MOQs above are typical starting points; the firm minimum depends on chip, size, finish and encoding, so we quote it in writing per program rather than post one number that is wrong for half of them.

sections.title: Buying direct vs a trading company — where the markup lives
sections.intro: A page about factory-direct pricing owes you an honest account of what the middleman actually does, and the answer is 'handle the transaction,' not 'improve the tag.' A trading company forwards your purchase order to a factory like this one, adds a margin for the service, and passes along a product it cannot inspect, modify or expedite — it owns no line to do any of those things. The point below is not that trading companies are villains; it is that you may be paying for a manufacturing capability your supplier does not have. When a credential carries your access-control or payment system, that gap is the whole game.

before: Your order is forwarded to a factory the desk does not own; you pay its price plus a resale margin.
Quality is whatever the unnamed plant shipped — the desk cannot inspect an inlay or retune an antenna it did not make.
Lead times and MOQs can move after you commit, because the desk is relaying someone else's schedule.
Technical questions bounce: the salesperson asks the factory, then relays an answer days later.
'Custom' means your logo on a stock tag; the chip and antenna were chosen for the desk's margin.
after: Your order reaches our production planner directly; you pay the factory-gate price with no resale layer.
Every encoded unit is 100% read-verified in-house, with a photographic QC report and the encoding log shipped alongside.
MOQ, price and lead time are quoted in writing before tooling, then held to the production traveler.
Engineering, quality and planning answer directly — the people who built the tag, not a message relay.
Custom means an engineered antenna, substrate and finish tuned to your surface and reader, not just print.

faq.question: How do I verify Proud Tek is a real factory and not a trading company?
faq.answer: Start by not treating an ISO certificate as proof of a factory — the scope line decides that, and it is the line most buyers skip. Ours are published rather than sent on request: ISO 9001 98026Q00274R000, ISO 14001 98026E00200R000, ISO 45001 98026S00203R000, registrar Anhui Certification and Inspection, valid to 09 June 2029, verifiable at zjcaic.com or cnca.gov.cn. Their certified scope is the sales service of smart cards and RFID tags, so they establish the legal entity and its management system — not the production floor. The check that settles the factory question is a site audit: book one across our Shenzhen sites in person or by live video walk-through, ask for the manufacturing site's own certification and audit documents by name, and bring third-party (SGS, TUV, Intertek) inspection if your program requires it. Then order a sample pack and put the parts on your own readers. A trading company cannot pass the second and third checks, because it owns no line to show you.

faq.question: How does buying direct compare with going through a trading company?
faq.answer: You pay the factory-gate price instead of that price plus a reseller's margin, and you gain a manufacturing capability the middleman does not have. A trading company forwards your order to a factory it does not own, so it cannot inspect an inlay, retune an antenna or expedite a run — it relays messages. Buying direct puts the engineering, quality and production-planning teams on the other end of your email, and makes one party accountable when a batch has to be reworked.

faq.question: What are your payment terms for a first order?
faq.answer: First orders typically run on a 30% deposit / 70% balance before shipment by T/T wire transfer, with PayPal and Alibaba Trade Assurance available for samples and small orders so a new buyer has payment protection. For larger commitments we open Letters of Credit; a common threshold is orders above $10,000. Exact terms are confirmed in writing per order — send your spec and target volume and you will have them alongside the quote.

faq.question: What is the minimum order quantity for factory-direct pricing?
faq.answer: Typical minimums start around 500 pieces for RFID cards and wristbands and 1,000 pieces for NFC stickers, labels and inlays, kept low because we hold running stock of popular chips and materials. The firm MOQ depends on chip, size, finish and encoding, so we quote it in writing per program. Samples always come first, so you qualify the part before committing to a minimum.

faq.question: Can you ship directly to my country, and on what Incoterms?
faq.answer: Yes — we export directly from Shenzhen to any country on DDP, FOB or CIF terms by DHL, FedEx or UPS express, or by ocean freight for volume. Because the goods leave our own factory, there is no extra handling hop through a trading company's warehouse; repeat buyers draw against safety stock with 3-5 business day call-offs.
